hints: Think back to the four different human malarias you met in infectious disease - one causes the most severe malignant malaria and the other three cause milder forms.
walkthrough:
Recall the human parasites**
Humans are infected by four distinct species in the genus Plasmodium. They all cause malaria but differ in severity. The best known is the one that causes severe, potentially fatal malignant malaria.

Give one correct binomial name**
Any one is correct: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium ovale or Plasmodium malariae. Remember to write the genus with a capital P and the species in lower case, ideally in italics.
Final answer: Plasmodium falciparum (accept P. vivax / P. ovale / P. malariae).

hints: Focus on which genus of mosquito can support the sexual stage of Plasmodium in its gut - it is not the same genus that spreads dengue or yellow fever.
walkthrough:
Link parasite to its second host**
Plasmodium needs two hosts to complete its life cycle: humans and a mosquito. Only one mosquito genus provides the right gut conditions for fertilisation and oocyst formation.

Name the genus**
That mosquito is Anopheles. Just the genus name is needed here, with a capital A.

hints: Start by thinking beyond magnification - a light image blown up large still looks blurry. What property decides whether two tiny close points are seen as separate?
Think about what illuminates each microscope and how wavelength controls that property, and what this means for seeing fine detail inside the oocyst.
walkthrough:
Magnification is not the same as resolution**
Both microscopes can magnify to the same size, but a light microscope image at high magnification becomes fuzzy. What matters is resolution, the ability to distinguish two very close points as separate.

Why electrons resolve more**
Resolution is limited by wavelength. Light has a relatively long wavelength with a resolution limit of about $200 \text{ nm}$ ($0.2 \mu\text{m}$). Electrons have a much shorter wavelength, giving a resolution of about $0.5 \text{ nm}$.

Apply to the oocyst image**
Because of that higher resolving power, the transmission electron microscope shows fine internal detail of the developing Plasmodium cells inside the oocyst that would be blurred or invisible with light, even at the same magnification.
Final answer: Electron microscope has higher resolution / resolving power than light microscope due to shorter wavelength of electrons; can distinguish between two close points and show more detail.

hints: First measure the printed length of the $20 \mu\text{m}$ scale bar in mm with a ruler - it should be about 10 mm on the paper.
Next remind yourself how to make the top and bottom of the fraction match - convert your mm measurement into $\mu\text{m}$ before dividing.
Now put it together using magnification = image length divided by actual length and work out the value with no units.
walkthrough:
Write the governing formula**
Use $$M = \frac{I}{A}$$ where $I$ is the measured image length of the scale bar and $A$ is the actual length it represents, here $20 \mu\text{m}$.

Measure and convert to common units**
Measure the scale bar on the printed Fig. 3.1. It is about $10 \text{ mm}$. Convert to micrometres: $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \mu\text{m}$, so $$10 \text{ mm} = 10 \times 1000 = 10000 \mu\text{m}$$

Substitute and calculate**
$$M = \frac{10000 \mu\text{m}}{20 \mu\text{m}} = 500$$ So magnification is $\times 500$. Magnification has no units because units cancel. Show formula, measurement, conversion and working to gain all 3 marks.
Final answer: magnification = image length / actual length = $10 \text{ mm} / 20 \mu\text{m} = 10000 \mu\text{m} / 20 \mu\text{m} = \times 500$.

hints: Think about the correct ecological term for a living carrier that passes a parasite between hosts without itself suffering the disease.
Now trace the feeding events - how does the mosquito first pick up the parasite in blood, and how do mature parasites later leave the mosquito to enter a new person?
walkthrough:
Acting as a vector**
The mosquito is the vector, the living transmitter between human hosts. It also acts as a host because part of the Plasmodium life cycle, including sexual reproduction and oocyst development, happens in its gut.

Pick up and pass on by feeding**
When a female feeds on blood of an infected person she takes up parasites. After development, mature Plasmodium cells move to the salivary glands. When she feeds again on an uninfected person, parasites in saliva / anticoagulant are injected with the saliva into the blood, starting a new infection.
Final answer: Mosquito acts as vector; takes up Plasmodium when feeding on blood of infected person; infective Plasmodium cells enter new person with saliva / anticoagulant when mosquito feeds.
